blocks.text: The first sheet of the national NZMS1 series, Napier and Hastings N134, appeared in March 1939. At one inch to one mile, it brought a consistent sheet layout and standard of national coverage. Its contours and features were compiled from survey information and aerial photographs.

blocks.text: The Second World War redirected much survey and mapping effort to defence. Field observations, existing control and aerial photographs fed into tactical and fortress-area mapping. Aerial photography helped mapmakers compile broad areas, while surveyors and draughtspeople still supplied control, interpretation and finished sheets.

blocks.text: After the war, the national topographic sheet became a base for engineering, science and administration. Roads, rivers, settlements, contours and named features were selected and generalised for the series’ scale. Consistent sheet numbers and place-name decisions helped users compare editions and locate the same area across the country.

blocks.text: Scale and purpose matter when layers are overlaid. A road shown on a national sheet is not a cadastral boundary; a contour is an interpreted line, not a surveyed point at every location. Similar-looking geometry can carry different evidence, accuracy and intended use.
